pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Someone hands you a slow feed endpoint and asks you to make it fast. Before you change a line, what do you do — and how do you read the load test you run?
expected_points: turn the request into a question with a number in it: rate, percentile, dataset size — "is it fast?" has no answer and no stopping condition
fix the dataset and warm up first; a service over 100 rows and the same service over ten million are different programs, and the first requests pay for empty pools and caches
read p50/p95/p99, never the mean — the mean hides the users you are losing, and percentiles compose: twenty calls per page against a p95 means roughly two page loads in three contain one
report throughput and error rate alongside latency; a fast p99 next to 30% 500s is not fast
drive at a fixed rate, not a closed loop — a generator that waits for each response throttles itself exactly when the service starts queueing, so the queue never forms
change one thing at a time and keep the baseline; a single benchmark run is noise (-count=10, benchstat)
pprof and benchmarks show where time and allocations went inside the process; the load test shows what the process looks like from outside

questions.prompt: The starter `Feed` asks the store for one author per article. Explain why that is a bug, how you proved it was fixed, and when you would join instead of batch.
expected_points: N+1: one query for the page plus one per row, so round trips scale with page size — 51 trips to serve 50 rows
it is the same bug as the GraphQL resolver N+1, one layer down; AuthorsByIDs is deliberately the dataloader's batch function without the queue
the proof is a count, not a stopwatch: the instrumented Store asserts exactly two round trips at limits 5, 20 and 50, and one for an empty feed
batch collapses duplicate ids (twenty articles by five authors is five parameters), omits missing rows rather than erroring, and makes no query at all for an empty list
join wins for one-to-one with small joined columns; batch wins when children are shared, when the child is a list (a join multiplies the result set), or when the two things live in different stores
the production version of that counter is a queries-per-request histogram beside the S5 request metrics

questions.prompt: Why did the feed move from `LIMIT ? OFFSET ?` to a cursor? Give me both reasons, and tell me what the cursor has to contain.
expected_points: speed: the database cannot jump to row 200,000 — it produces and discards them all, so cost grows with depth, and keyset seeks to an anchor and reads LIMIT rows at constant cost

correctness: OFFSET counts rows, so inserts at the head push the window back and page 2 repeats page 1 (deletes make it skip rows, which nobody notices) — a cursor is anchored to a row, so it cannot shift
the sort key must be unique: created_at alone straddles ties, so the cursor carries (created_at, id) and the comparison is on the pair
the index must match the ordering — an index is a promise about one access pattern, not a speed setting
ask the planner: the row-value form plans as SEARCH into articles_feed, the logically identical OR form plans as a SCAN, which is correctness with no speed
make it opaque (base64) so clients cannot depend on its shape — opaque is not secret, so validate it (bad cursor is a 400) and always bind it as a parameter
what it costs: no jump-to-page-57, no free total count, and re-sorting means redesigning the cursor

questions.prompt: Walk me through your `GET /articles` response headers. What does the ETag say, what does `Cache-Control` say, and what actually gets saved when a client comes back with `If-None-Match`?
expected_points: the ETag names *what* this representation is; Cache-Control says *who* may keep it and *for how long* — two different statements
hashing the body is the tag that cannot be wrong; a cheaper tag from a version column or updated_at must account for every input that changes the output, including the one added next quarter
If-None-Match matching means 304 with no body — and the validators go on the 304 too, or the client's copy has no tag and no lifetime and the next request comes back unconditional
comparison is weak: `*` matches anything non-empty, the header is a comma-separated list, and W/"abc" matches "abc"
a 304 saves bandwidth, not work, unless something above it stopped you rebuilding the body
public means "the same for everybody" — get it wrong on a session-scoped response and a shared cache hands one user's data to the next; use private, and Vary when the body depends on a request header
no-cache means revalidate before reuse, not "do not cache"; no-store is the one for tokens

questions.prompt: Your `Cache` is a map with a mutex. Why does it also need a TTL, an entry bound, and a `Purge` on the write path — and what changes about all of that when you run three replicas?
expected_points: TTL bounds staleness (how wrong an answer may be); the entry bound bounds memory, and it is mandatory because the key is built from client-controlled limit and cursor — otherwise a stranger fills the heap one distinct key at a time
an expired entry read is a miss *and* a removal, or cold keys hold their bytes for as long as there is room
Purge is correctness, not tuning: without it a client does not see its own write for the whole TTL and reports the API as losing data
cache the rendered bytes with their tag, not the struct — a hit that still marshals and hashes gives back most of what it saved
hits/misses are the instrument: a cache with no hit rate is a guess with a mutex, and a hit rate that collapses after a deploy usually means a key grew a new dimension

three replicas: each sees a third of the traffic so hit rates fall, you hold three copies, and a purge on the writing replica leaves the other two stale until their own TTL — fine, but say the number out loud ("at most 30 s stale")
the alternative is a cache outside the process, which is another thing to run, monitor and invalidate
a hot key expiring is a stampede; single-flight, jittered TTLs or serve-stale-while-refreshing are the cures

questions.prompt: You may ship one change this week: add the cache, fix the N+1, or switch to keyset pagination. Which goes first, why, and what evidence would move you?
expected_points: the order is: stop doing unnecessary work → fix the query shape → then cache → then the payload
unnecessary work (N+1, a missing index, columns you drop, COUNT(*) per page) is where the order-of-magnitude wins are and none of it costs correctness

caching first hides the problems underneath it until the cache misses — and it misses precisely when you are busiest: a deploy, a purge, a stampede; a cache in front of a bad query is a slow query with worse failure modes
caching also buys staleness, which is a product decision, where removing round trips buys nothing back
the evidence is specific: queries per request, the query plan (SCAN where you expected SEARCH), and p95/p99 at a fixed rate before and after — one change at a time
if the numbers say the endpoint is read-dominated and already minimal, caching does move to the front; the answer is defensible either way only with data

questions.prompt: Two dials people reach for: raising `SetMaxOpenConns` and turning on gzip. When does each make things worse?
expected_points: MaxOpenConns is a concurrency limit, not a speed setting — past what the database can do at once you buy contention, context switches and memory, and throughput falls while latency rises

round numbers: a 5 ms query over 10 connections retires about 2,000 queries a second; more concurrency does not create capacity, it moves the wait into your process where db.Stats().WaitCount and WaitDuration make it visible
a bounded pool is a bulkhead protecting the database from your service, and a queue you can see beats a database you cannot
MaxIdleConns should usually equal MaxOpenConns, and ConnMaxLifetime rotates connections so a failover or an idle timeout does not hand you a dead one
gzip below ~1 KB can add bytes; it never compresses JPEG/PNG/MP4/zip; it always costs CPU on both ends, so it lowers throughput on a CPU-bound service and is nearly free on a database-bound one
Vary: Accept-Encoding is mandatory or a shared cache serves gzip to a client that asked for none
BREACH: do not compress a response mixing secrets with attacker-influenced content
often the right answer is neither hand-rolled middleware nor a dependency — let the reverse proxy or CDN do it

questions.prompt: The database is no longer the bottleneck and the endpoint is still not fast enough. What is left, and where do those techniques fight each other?
expected_points: select only what you return (the feed omits article bodies): columns you drop cost wire bytes, driver memory and client parse time
precompute at write time — a maintained counter beats COUNT(*) per read, and reads usually outnumber writes by an order of magnitude
do startup work at startup: compile regexps and templates once
reuse buffers (sync.Pool, a reused bytes.Buffer) *after* pprof -alloc_objects says allocation is the problem, not before

stream with json.NewEncoder(w) instead of building the whole body with json.Marshal — but you cannot hash a body you did not buffer, so ETags and streaming pull against each other: buffer and tag small responses, stream large ones untagged
cache rendered bytes rather than structs, for the same reason
these are single-digit-percent moves once the big ones are gone, and worth having then — measured, one at a time
